question: A 6-month-old infant presents with poor feeding, excessive sweating during feeds, and recurrent chest infections. Examination reveals a pansystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border, a thrill, and hepatomegaly. Which haemodynamic mechanism best explains this clinical picture?

answers.text: Right-to-left shunting causing systemic deoxygenation and central cyanosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Right-to-left shunting characterises cyanotic CHD (e.g. TOF). In acyanotic defects such as VSD, the shunt direction is left-to-right because systemic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure.

answers.text: Left-to-right shunting causing pulmonary overcirculation and volume overload of the left heart

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In VSD, blood shunts from the high-pressure left ventricle to the right ventricle, increasing pulmonary blood flow. This volume-loads the pulmonary vasculature and left heart, causing failure symptoms: sweating, poor feeding, recurrent infections, and hepatomegaly.

answers.text: Fixed obstruction to right ventricular outflow causing right-sided pressure overload

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Obstructive lesions (e.g. pulmonary stenosis) cause pressure overload but not the pulmonary plethora, volume overload, and failure symptoms seen here. A pansystolic murmur at LLSB indicates a shunt defect, not outflow obstruction.

answers.text: Ductal-dependent systemic circulation resulting in differential cyanosis of the lower limbs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Differential cyanosis (lower limbs more cyanosed than upper limbs) is pathognomonic of reversed-PDA Eisenmenger syndrome, not the initial presentation of an unrepaired VSD in infancy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the haemodynamics of left-to-right shunt lesions. The key: systemic pressure > pulmonary pressure in acyanotic CHD pushes blood from left to right, flooding the pulmonary circuit.
Well done. L-R shunting → pulmonary overcirculation → volume overload is the central haemodynamic concept for acyanotic shunt defects.
